## Quick start[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#quick-start)

The shortest walk through the door: a framework-free PHP page and the `fake` driver, which needs no server and no registration. Every snippet below is the [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html) example, one move at a time.

1. **Require the package.**
   ```
   composer require waynestate/sesame
   ```
   Expected: `waynestate/sesame` is in `composer.json` and installed in `vendor/`.
2. **Start the session.** The app owns the session; SESAME never starts one.
   ```php
   <?php
   
   declare(strict_types=1);
   
   require __DIR__.'/vendor/autoload.php';
   
   session_start();
   ```
   Note
   Set `session.gc_maxlifetime` to at least SESAME's idle timeout. PHP's default is 1440 seconds (24 minutes), and PHP's garbage collector deletes session data older than that, so on the defaults a raw-PHP app signs people out after 24 quiet minutes, long before SESAME's 120-minute idle timeout. Set `session.gc_maxlifetime = 7200` (your `session.idle_minutes` times 60) in `php.ini` or the FPM pool, or call `ini_set('session.gc_maxlifetime', '7200')` before `session_start()`.
   Expected: the session is started, and the autoload file sees the package.
3. **Configure the `fake` driver for local development.**
   ```php
   use Waynestate\Sesame\Config;
   
   $config = Config::fromArray([
       'driver' => 'fake',
       'environment' => 'local',
       'fake' => [
           'username' => 'jdoe',
           'attributes' => ['cn' => ['John Doe']],
       ],
   ]);
   ```
   Expected: `$config` names the `fake` driver, the local environment, and the identity the driver will return.
4. **Build the facade and hand it to the functions.**
   ```php
   use Waynestate\Sesame\DriverFactory;
   use Waynestate\Sesame\Identity;
   use Waynestate\Sesame\Sesame;
   use Waynestate\Sesame\Session\NativeSession;
   use Waynestate\Sesame\UserResolver;
   
   $sesame = new Sesame(
       DriverFactory::make($config),
       new class implements UserResolver {
           public function findOrImportUser(Identity $identity): mixed
           {
               return $identity->username;
           }
       },
       new NativeSession(),
       $config,
   );
   
   sesame($sesame);
   ```
   Expected: no output. The next call has a driver, a resolver, a session and a config to work with.
5. **Sign the user in.**
   ```php
   $user = sesame_login();
   ```
   Expected: when the login has not completed, SESAME sends the redirect to the identity provider and stops the script; when a ticket completes it, it sends the redirect to the driver's service URL and stops the script, so the ticket never stays in the address bar; when the user is already signed in and the request has no ticket, it returns the user. With the `fake` driver, that user is the one your resolver made from `jdoe`.
6. **Read the user on a protected page.**
   ```php
   $user = sesame_user();
   ```
   Expected: the user the login stored in the session.

### What you built[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#what-you-built)

A framework-free PHP page that signs a user in through SESAME and reads the signed-in user back out of the session. The protocol never held the session: you started it and you read it, and switching driver is a config change with no code change.

### Next steps[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html#next-steps)

- [Which driver for my app?](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html): pick the key for your real door.
- [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html): the whole example, with every piece named.
- [Laravel](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html): the same door in a Laravel app.
- [Session timeouts](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html): the two clocks every session runs on.

---

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html

## Raw PHP[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#raw-php)

This page shows how a framework-free PHP app boots SESAME, signs the user in, reads the user back, and signs the user out. Start with the boot example, then wire up your protected pages.

### Boot the app[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#boot-the-app)

```php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

require __DIR__.'/vendor/autoload.php';

use Waynestate\Sesame\Config;
use Waynestate\Sesame\DriverFactory;
use Waynestate\Sesame\Identity;
use Waynestate\Sesame\Sesame;
use Waynestate\Sesame\Session\NativeSession;
use Waynestate\Sesame\UserResolver;

session_start();

$config = Config::fromArray([
    'driver' => 'fake',
    'environment' => 'local',
    'fake' => [
        'username' => 'jdoe',
        'attributes' => ['cn' => ['John Doe']],
    ],
]);

$sesame = new Sesame(
    DriverFactory::make($config),
    new class implements UserResolver {
        public function findOrImportUser(Identity $identity): mixed
        {
            return $identity->username;
        }
    },
    new NativeSession(),
    $config,
);

sesame($sesame);

// When the login has not completed, sends the redirect to the identity
// provider and stops the script. When a ticket completes it, sends the
// redirect to the driver's service URL and stops the script, so the ticket
// never stays in the address bar. When the user is already signed in and
// the request has no ticket, returns the user.
$user = sesame_login();
```

### Which key to store[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#which-key-to-store)

Your `findOrImportUser` looks the person up in the app's own store, so key that store on the driver plus the identity provider's own stable identifier, never on an email or a display name, which can change or be shared between providers. For the cas driver that identifier is the `username` (the Access ID), so the key is `$identity->driver` plus `$identity->username`. Other drivers name their stable identifier differently: the oidc section keys on `iss` plus `sub`, or `tid` plus `oid`, never the username alone.

### Session ownership[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#session-ownership)

The app owns the session: start it with `session_start()`, and let HELMET set the cookie flags. SESAME regenerates the session ID on login and stores the user and identity in it, but it never starts a session and never touches a cookie. `sesame_login()` and `sesame_logout()` stop the script after they send their redirect, so nothing after them runs in that request. A protected page reads the user with `sesame_user()`:

```php
$user = sesame_user();
```

Warning

**Set `session.gc_maxlifetime` to at least SESAME's idle timeout.** PHP's default is 1440 seconds (24 minutes), and PHP's garbage collector deletes session data older than that, so a raw-PHP app on the defaults signs people out after 24 quiet minutes, long before SESAME's 120-minute idle timeout. SESAME never starts the session (S2), so it cannot change this for you: set `session.gc_maxlifetime = 7200` (your `session.idle_minutes` times 60) in `php.ini` or the FPM pool, or call `ini_set('session.gc_maxlifetime', '7200')` before `session_start()`. SESAME's timeouts stay the authority; this only stops PHP from ending the session first. Laravel apps set `SESSION_LIFETIME` (minutes) instead.

### The session cookie (name and SameSite)[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#the-session-cookie-name-and-samesite)

SESAME never sets a cookie, so two choices belong to the session setup. In raw PHP HELMET makes both for you (`SessionHardening::apply()`, called by `helmet_boot()`); in Laravel they are settings in `config/session.php`:

- **Name it with the `__Host-` prefix** (S4). The browser then accepts the cookie only if it is `Secure`, has `Path=/` and has no `Domain`, so a sibling subdomain under `*.apps.wayne.edu` cannot overwrite it. HELMET names the cookie `__Host-WSUSESSID` on HTTPS (it keeps a name your app chose). In Laravel, set `SESSION_COOKIE=__Host-wsu-session`, `SESSION_SECURE_COOKIE=true`, `SESSION_PATH=/` and leave `SESSION_DOMAIN` empty in `config/session.php`.
- **Keep it `SameSite=Lax`, never `Strict`** (S41). The identity provider sends the browser back to your app with a cross-site top-level `GET`, and a `Strict` cookie is not sent on that request: it would be missing, so the app would see no session on the return request and any login binding (S18) would fail for every user. `Lax` is what HELMET sets and what Laravel does by default. A cross-site `POST` carries no `Lax` cookie at all, which is the defense you want; that is why the `saml` driver's ACS page parks the IdP's POST without a session and sends the browser back to the login URL with a 303, where the `Lax` cookie is sent again (S35; see [The saml driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-saml.html)).
- **Leave the session ID length alone** (S45). Do not set `session.sid_length` or `session.sid_bits_per_character`: PHP's default ID is 32 hexadecimal characters (128 bits), and on PHP 8.4 and later both settings are deprecated and raise notices. A low value weakens the ID. Neither SESAME nor HELMET sets or checks them.

On logout, both paths send `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "storage"` so a back button or a shared browser cannot show a signed-in page; `"cookies"` is left out on purpose, because it would clear every cookie on the host and sign the user out of every other app on wayne.edu, not just this one. Single logout is not supported, the identity provider cannot sign the user out of the app's other sessions, so SESAME rejects a truthy `slo` (or `single_logout`) config key at boot.

### Logout[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#logout)

Logout is POST-only, with a CSRF token. `sesame_logout()` runs only for a POST whose body carries the session's `sesame_logout_token`; a GET answers 405 (`Allow: POST`) and a POST without the right token answers 403, and both leave the session alone. So another site cannot sign the user out with an image, a link or a forged form. Put the token in the sign-out form:

```php
<form method="post" action="/logout.php">
  <input type="hidden" name="sesame_logout_token" value="<?= sesame_logout_token() ?>">
  <button>Sign out</button>
</form>
```

```php
// logout.php
sesame_logout('https://app.example.test/');
```

The token lives in the session, is made on first use and dies with the session at logout. Laravel apps use Laravel's own CSRF token instead: the `POST /logout` route is in the `web` middleware group, so a form needs `@csrf`.

### Helper functions[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#helper-functions)

The raw-PHP path is a set of plain functions in the global namespace behind a `sesame_` prefix, each guarded with `function_exists` so two copies of the file can never collide. The app owns the session: start it with `session_start()` before calling anything here, and let HELMET set the cookie flags.

| Function | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `sesame(?Sesame $instance = null)` | Hold the one `Sesame` instance for this process: pass the instance to set it, pass nothing to read it. Throws `LogicException` when read before it is set. |
| `sesame_request()` | Build the PSR-7 request for the current request from the globals, using the `nyholm/psr7` factories the library already requires. |
| `sesame_login(): mixed` | Run a login against the current request. Sends the 302 and stops the script when the driver answers with a redirect; returns the app's user, or `null` when the resolver refused the identity. |
| `sesame_user(): mixed` | The app's user for the current session, or `null` when there is none. |
| `sesame_require_mfa(int $maxAgeSeconds = 28800): mixed` | Require that the signed-in user's MFA is still good. Returns the user when satisfied, throws `MfaNotSatisfied` otherwise. |
| `sesame_require_context(string $id): mixed` | Require that the signed-in identity has the given authentication context. Returns the user when it does, throws `AuthContextNotSatisfied` otherwise. |
| `sesame_logout_token(): string` | The logout CSRF token for this session, for the logout form. The token is hex, so it needs no escaping in HTML. |
| `sesame_logout(string $returnTo): void` | Log the user out, then send them on. Invalidates the app session, redirects to the identity provider's logout URL when the driver has one, otherwise to the safe return-to, and stops the script. |

### Logging[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#logging)

The facade takes an optional sixth constructor argument: a PSR-3 logger (`Psr\Log\LoggerInterface`). When you pass one, SESAME writes one record per authentication event through it:

| Event | Level | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `sesame.login` | `info` | A verified identity resolved to a user and the session was stored. |
| `sesame.login_failed` | `warning` | The driver's login threw `AuthenticationFailed`. |
| `sesame.login_refused` | `warning` | The resolver refused the identity and returned null. |
| `sesame.logout` | `info` | The session was signed out (a logout, a timeout, or a deleted user). |
| `sesame.session_anomaly` | `warning` | The session state looks wrong or tampered with: `reason` is `missing_timestamps` or `bad_session_ref`. |

Each record carries `event`, `driver`, `username` and `at` (the time in UTC) in its context, and `sesame.logout` adds `reason` (`logout`, `idle_timeout`, `absolute_timeout`, `no_timestamps` or `user_gone`). `sesame.session_anomaly` adds `reason` (`missing_timestamps`, a user stored without the session's timestamps, or `bad_session_ref`, a stored reference that is not the 16-character lowercase hex value login created) and carries `session_ref` when the stored value is still a valid 16-character lowercase hex string; when you see one, look at the `session_ref` and the user around it in the log to see what happened to the session. `sesame.login` and `sesame.logout` also carry `session_ref`: an opaque 16-character hex reference SESAME creates on every login (stored in the session under `sesame.session_ref`) that ties the login, timeouts and logout of one sign-in together in the log. It is not the session ID and never derived from it, and a value read back from the session that is not a 16-character lowercase hex string is ignored, so a tampered session cannot inject log text. The logger stays optional: without one, nothing is logged and nothing else changes.

SESAME never logs tickets, session IDs, tokens or failure messages: a failed login records only the event, the driver and the time. Usernames have every control character replaced with `?` and are cut at 128 characters, so a username cannot forge an extra log line or flood the log. A logger that throws never changes what the facade returns or throws.

### Related[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html#related)

- [Which driver for my app?](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html)
- [WSU values (Playbook)](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html)

---

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html

## Requiring MFA[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html#requiring-mfa)

Open sesame opens the door; requiring MFA checks the key is still in the lock. A signed-in session is not the same as a recently-verified one, so a protected page can ask for proof that the user's MFA is still good, not just that they are signed in. This page is the rule itself and how to apply it from raw PHP or Laravel; next, see [Step-up (authentication context)](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html) for asking the identity provider for a stronger sign-in.

### The rule[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html#the-rule)

The check reads two facts from the identity: `authTime`, when the user last completed MFA, and `amr`, the methods they used. It is satisfied when the identity has an `authTime` that is not in the future, is not older than the allowed age, and the `amr` includes an MFA method. It fails closed: no `authTime`, no MFA method, or an age that has passed all deny the request. Anything the provider did not report is treated as missing, so a driver that carries no MFA facts is always denied.

The checks run in a fixed order, so the reason is stable:

| Order | Reason | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `NO_AUTH_TIME` | The identity has no `authTime`. |
| 2 | `FUTURE_AUTH_TIME` | `authTime` sits more than 60 seconds in the future (a clock problem). |
| 3 | `TOO_OLD` | `authTime` is older than the allowed age. |
| 4 | `NO_MFA_METHOD` | The `amr` list carries no method that counts as MFA. |
| 5 | `SATISFIED` | All of the above pass. |

A sign-in exactly the allowed age old is still satisfied. The allowed age defaults to eight hours (`28800` seconds).

### MFA methods[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html#mfa-methods)

The `amr` values that count as MFA:

| MFA method | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `mfa` | A generic MFA step. |
| `otp` | A one-time password. |
| `hwk` | A hardware key. |
| `swk` | A software key. |
| `fido` | A FIDO/WebAuthn assertion. |
| `sms` | A one-time code by SMS. |
| `pop` | A possession proof. |

### Raw PHP[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html#raw-php)

In raw PHP, a protected page reads the user and the MFA proof in one call:

```php
// Throws MfaNotSatisfied when the MFA check is not satisfied.
$user = sesame_require_mfa();
```

Or, with a custom max age:

```php
$user = sesame_require_mfa(3600);
```

The core method returns the result instead of throwing:

```php
$result = $sesame->requireMfa();

if (! $result->satisfied) {
    // $result->reason is a stable code; $result->message() is the human text.
}
```

### Which drivers carry MFA facts[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html#which-drivers-carry-mfa-facts)

The gateway and oidc drivers report MFA facts from the token's `auth_time` and `amr` claims (the oidc driver also has `oidc.assume_mfa`, see [The oidc driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-oidc.html)). The cas driver reports none by default, because CAS carries no usable MFA signal, so a cas identity fails the check. With `cas.assume_mfa` on, a cas identity carries `mfa` in its `amr` and its MFA time from the CAS `authenticationDate` attribute, so the check can pass when the CAS server enforces MFA for every sign-in.

Warning

Turn on `cas.assume_mfa` only when the CAS server enforces MFA for every sign-in. Ask your CAS server's owner before turning it on; a server that enforces MFA only sometimes, or only for some users, would make the MFA check pass for sign-ins that never did MFA.

### In Laravel[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html#in-laravel)

Require MFA on a route with the `sesame.mfa` middleware:

```php
Route::get('/vault', fn () => view('vault'))->middleware(['auth.sesame', 'sesame.mfa']);
```

It lets the request through when the signed-in user's MFA is still good, and otherwise stops it: a 403 by default, a JSON 403 for JSON requests, and a redirect to the login route when `mfa.on_failure` is `reauth`. The allowed age comes from the route parameter when there is one, and from `mfa.max_age` when there is not:

```php
Route::get('/vault', fn () => view('vault'))->middleware(['auth.sesame', 'sesame.mfa:3600']);
```

The `mfa.on_failure` setting picks what a failed check does: `deny` (the default) answers a 403, and `reauth` sends the user back to the login route. With the oidc driver, `reauth` asks the provider for a step-up, so the user comes back with a fresh `auth_time`; see [Step-up (authentication context)](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html).

### Related[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html#related)

- [Session timeouts](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html)
- [The oidc driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-oidc.html)
- [The cas driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-cas.html)
- [The gateway driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-gateway.html)
- [Laravel](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html)
- [Step-up (authentication context)](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html)

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/running-off-citadel.html

## Running off Citadel[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/running-off-citadel.html#running-off-citadel)

This page is the checklist for running an SESAME app off Citadel, on OpenShift, Coolify or raw Docker. Read the three topics below in order, because each one is a config change, not a code change.

Open sesame opens the door on any host, not just Citadel. SESAME takes its config from the app (env or `config/sesame.php`), keeps no files of its own, and has no platform address in code, so a move to OpenShift, Coolify or raw Docker is a config change, not a code change. What differs per host:

### The cas driver[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/running-off-citadel.html#the-cas-driver)

The `cas` driver needs outbound HTTPS from the app to the CAS server, and `service_url` must be the public URL users see, behind any proxy.

### The gateway driver[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/running-off-citadel.html#the-gateway-driver)

The `gateway` driver trusts only a signed assertion, never a bare header. A source address is not enough on its own: on shared ingress (OpenShift's router, Coolify's Traefik) the same proxy carries routes with and without the auth step. The header name and the list of trusted auth hops are config.

Its replay guard remembers used `jti`s in a cache store, so that store must be shared too (Redis or a database), for the same reason as the session store: a local-file cache would let a replayed assertion pass on another replica.

Warning

A local-file replay store is unsafe on a multi-replica host: a replayed assertion would pass on another replica. Share the store (Redis or a database).

### The session store[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/running-off-citadel.html#the-session-store)

The session store must be shared: Redis or a database, never local files. Every host overlaps old and new containers during a deploy, and most can run more than one replica, so a file session would drop users mid-login. In Laravel, set `SESSION_DRIVER` to `redis` or `database` (Laravel 13 already defaults to `database`); in raw PHP, set `session.save_handler` to a shared handler, for example Redis.

### Related[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/running-off-citadel.html#related)

- [The cas driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-cas.html)
- [The gateway driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-gateway.html)

---

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html

## Session timeouts[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html#session-timeouts)

Open sesame opens the door for a live session; a stale one finds it locked. This page is about the two clocks every signed-in session runs on and the settings that control them. When you have tuned them, see [Requiring MFA](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html), which ages the sign-in time the same clocks record.

### The two clocks[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html#the-two-clocks)

Every signed-in session has two clocks. The idle timeout is the quiet time after which the session is dropped, and the absolute lifetime is the longest a session may live, no matter how active it is. Both are in minutes, and both are checked on every `user()` call, so a stale session is signed out on the spot the first time anything asks who is signed in.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `session.idle_minutes` | `120` | Drop the session after this much quiet time. |
| `session.absolute_minutes` | `720` | End the session this long after sign-in, even if it is still active. |
| `logoutReuseTtlSeconds` | `60` | The window in which a reused logged-out session ID is logged as an anomaly, in seconds. A `new NativeSession()` option, not a config key; `0` makes `invalidate()` destroy the session outright instead of leaving the logout marker. |

### How the clocks are checked[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html#how-the-clocks-are-checked)

On login the session stores the sign-in time and the last activity time, and `user()` refreshes the last activity time on every call that finds a live session. A session made before the timeouts existed (a user, no timestamps) counts as expired.

### Regeneration grace[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html#regeneration-grace)

On login the session ID is regenerated. For the native PHP session the old ID is not deleted at once: it is marked with a "destroyed at" time and the new ID and kept for a 60 second grace, so a user whose browser is still sending the old ID after a slow network does not lose the login. After the grace, any use of the old ID is treated as a possible hijack: the session is retired, a clean one is started, and `sesame.session_anomaly` is logged as a warning with `reason` `destroyed_session_reused`. Pass `graceSeconds: 0` to `new NativeSession()` to restore the old behavior, where the old session is deleted at once. Laravel uses the framework's own regenerate.

### Logout reuse window[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html#logout-reuse-window)

When `invalidate()` retires a session it leaves a "logged out at" marker in the session store itself, under the same ID. The marker lives in the store, not in process memory, so no extra cache is needed and every worker sees the same marker. A later request that presents that ID is not revived: the marked session is retired, a fresh empty one starts, and while the reuse window lasts (60 seconds by default, the `logoutReuseTtlSeconds` option of `new NativeSession()`) the reuse is logged once with `reason` `logged_out_session_reused`. Past the window the marked session is still retired, just not logged. Pass `logoutReuseTtlSeconds: 0` to turn the check off: the session is destroyed outright on logout, the old behavior.

### In Laravel[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html#in-laravel)

In Laravel the keys are `SESAME_SESSION_IDLE_MINUTES` and `SESAME_SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MINUTES`.

### Related[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html#related)

- [Requiring MFA](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html)
- [Step-up (authentication context)](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html)
- [Laravel](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html)
- [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html)

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html

## Single-page apps[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#single-page-apps)

A single-page app that renders its own signed-in state needs a JSON answer to "who is signed in?". This page is about that answer: where it comes from, what it contains, and how to keep it honest. When you have wired it up, see [Session timeouts](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html), which explains the two expiries the answer carries.

### The two endpoints[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#the-two-endpoints)

SESAME answers the question two ways: `sesame_status()` in raw PHP and the `GET /sesame/status` route in Laravel. Both send the session facts with a 200 when someone is signed in, and `{"signedIn":false}` with a 401 when no one is:

```json
{
    "signedIn": true,
    "username": "jdoe",
    "driver": "cas",
    "authenticatedAt": "2026-11-03T09:15:00+00:00",
    "authTime": null,
    "amr": [],
    "idleExpiresAt": "2026-11-03T11:15:00+00:00",
    "absoluteExpiresAt": "2026-11-04T09:15:00+00:00",
    "logoutToken": "3f7a1c9e8b2d4a6f",
    "user": null
}
```

and, when signed out:

```json
{"signedIn":false}
```

The times are always UTC. Every answer carries `Cache-Control: no-store`, `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, so a browser or proxy never caches who is signed in.

### In raw PHP[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#in-raw-php)

Put the function at the end of a small endpoint script, after the same bootstrap a protected page uses:

```php
// status.php
require __DIR__.'/bootstrap.php'; // your usual session_start() and sesame($sesame)

sesame_status();
```

`sesame_status()` stops the script after the answer, so nothing after it runs in that request. Only GET (and HEAD) ask the question; any other method answers 405 (`Allow: GET, HEAD`) and leaves the session alone.

### In Laravel[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#in-laravel)

The route is registered with the login and logout routes (in the `web` group, so the session is available; a GET needs no CSRF token), and `SESAME_ROUTES=false` takes it away with them. The app's SPA reads `/sesame/status` directly.

### With Vue[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#with-vue)

This repo ships a thin Vue adapter for the answer: the [`vue/` folder](https://git.wayne.edu/enterprise-apps/sesame/-/blob/main/vue/README.md) gives you `useSesame()` (or `createSesame()` as an app-wide plugin) with reactive `signedIn`, `user` and `expired`, a `refresh()` for real user actions, and a `logout()` that posts the sign-out form. It never polls, for the reason below.

### Read it on page load, not on a timer[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#read-it-on-page-load-not-on-a-timer)

A poll counts as activity: reading the status moves the session's `last_seen`, so polling on a timer would keep a session alive past the idle timeout. Read it when the app loads and after a sign-in, and let the `idleExpiresAt` and `absoluteExpiresAt` in the answer tell you how long the state can be trusted.

### Adding your own user fields[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#adding-your-own-user-fields)

Pass a closure that returns an array of extra fields for the app's user: `sesame_status(fn ($user) => ['name' => $user->name])` in raw PHP, or bind the closure as `sesame.describe_user` in Laravel. Its array fills the answer's `user` field (null without a closure); the session facts stay untouched, and the identity provider's raw attributes are never part of the answer.

### Signing out[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#signing-out)

In raw PHP, nothing more is needed: `sesame_logout()` checks the form's `sesame_logout_token` against the answer's `logoutToken`. In Laravel the `POST /logout` route is in the `web` group, so the layout needs `<meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrf_token() }}">` (the Vue adapter's `logout()` reads it and sends it as `_token`; pass `csrfToken` to override).

### Related[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/single-page-apps.html#related)

- [Session timeouts](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/session-timeouts.html)
- [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html)
- [Laravel](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html)

---

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html

## Step-up (authentication context)[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html#step-up-authentication-context)

Open sesame opens the door; step-up checks the user actually walked through the right one. This page is how a step-up travels from the identity provider onto the identity, how to check it on a protected page, and which parameters a step-up request adds. Next, see [Requiring MFA](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html) for the age check on the same facts.

### What a step-up is[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html#what-a-step-up-is)

When the gateway requires a step-up for a path, it says so in the signed assertion's `acrs` claim, a list of authentication context ids (`c1` through `c99`). The gateway driver reads that claim and keeps only the ids of the right shape; anything else is dropped, and a missing or malformed claim is not an error, it is simply no step-up.

The contexts live on the identity, and the check is membership, never a prefix match: an identity with `c2` and `c10` satisfies `c2` and `c10`, but not `c1`.

```php
$identity->authContexts();      // list<string>, e.g. ['c1']
$identity->hasAuthContext('c1'); // bool
```

### Checking the context[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html#checking-the-context)

In raw PHP, a protected page reads the user and the context proof in one call:

```php
// Throws AuthContextNotSatisfied when the identity lacks the context.
$user = sesame_require_context('c1');
```

The core method returns a bool instead of throwing:

```php
if (! $sesame->hasAuthContext('c1')) {
    // The signed-in identity does not have the required context.
}
```

In Laravel the `sesame.context` middleware does the same check on a route:

```php
Route::get('/vault', [VaultController::class, 'index'])
    ->middleware(['web', 'auth.sesame', 'sesame.context:c1']);
```

A request without the context gets a 403, or a JSON 403 with a `message` for JSON requests. A route that names no context fails closed.

### Asking for a step-up (the oidc driver)[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html#asking-for-a-step-up-the-oidc-driver)

With the oidc driver, a login request with `step_up=1` adds the app's configured step-up parameters: `prompt=login` by default, and optionally `max_age`, `acr_values` and `claims`. The request can ask for a step-up but cannot choose what it is; only config feeds those values. The callback then requires a fresh `auth_time`: not in the future (beyond the leeway), not before the sign-in started when `prompt=login` was sent, and within `max_age`, which is 300 seconds when `oidc.step_up.max_age` is not set, so a step-up is never unbounded.

A page that needs fresh credentials sends the user to `login.php?step_up=1` in raw PHP. In Laravel, `sesame.mfa` with `mfa.on_failure=reauth` sends the user to `/login?step_up=1` for you.

#### Config keys[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html#config-keys)

| Key | Env | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `oidc.step_up.prompt` | `SESAME_OIDC_STEP_UP_PROMPT` | `login` | Sent on a step-up only; `login` or empty. |
| `oidc.step_up.max_age` | `SESAME_OIDC_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE` | none (300 enforced) | Seconds; sent on a step-up only, and enforced on `auth_time`. Unset, it is not sent, but a step-up `auth_time` older than 300 seconds still fails. |
| `oidc.step_up.acr_values` | `SESAME_OIDC_STEP_UP_ACR_VALUES` | none | Sent on a step-up only. |
| `oidc.step_up.claims` | `SESAME_OIDC_STEP_UP_CLAIMS` | none | A JSON object (for example an `acrs` request for an Entra authentication context), sent on a step-up only. |

### Which drivers report contexts[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html#which-drivers-report-contexts)

The gateway and oidc drivers report authentication contexts (the oidc driver from the ID token's `acrs` claim, after a step-up that asked for one through `oidc.step_up.claims`). A cas identity has none, so a cas identity always fails the check.

Note

The `acrs` claim feeds `hasAuthContext()`, while `auth_time` and `amr` feed the MFA check. They are separate facts: a context says the sign-in went through a stronger path, and the MFA facts say when and how.

### Related[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/step-up.html#related)

- [Requiring MFA](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/requiring-mfa.html)
- [The oidc driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-oidc.html)
- [The gateway driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-gateway.html)
- [Laravel](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html)

## Which driver for my app?[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html#which-driver-for-my-app)

One lock, any key: this page matches your situation to the right SESAME driver and tells you whether the app needs its own Entra registration. Pick the row that fits, then set that driver in your config.

### Match your situation[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html#match-your-situation)

| Situation | Driver | Entra registration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| App on Citadel today | `cas` | None. |
| App on Citadel once Drawbridge is live | `gateway` | None per app (Drawbridge holds it once). |
| App off Citadel or an API with its own audience | `oidc` or `oauth2` | Its own registration. |
| App that must sign in through a SAML IdP (Shibboleth-style), opt-in | `saml` | None; the IdP's administrators register the app's SP metadata instead. |
| Local development | `fake` | None. |

### The recommended path on Citadel[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html#the-recommended-path-on-citadel)

The recommended path on Citadel is the `gateway` driver behind Drawbridge. Drawbridge is Wayne State's auth gateway: the browser signs in once at the gateway, which passes the app a signed assertion that the `gateway` driver verifies. Drawbridge is not live yet, so there is no production gateway to point at today. Until it is, CAS (the `cas` driver) is today's option for a Citadel app, and it needs no per-app Entra registration.

### Related[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html#related)

- [WSU values (Playbook)](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html)
- [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html)
- [The saml driver](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-saml.html)

---

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html

## WSU values (Playbook)[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html#wsu-values-playbook)

These four settings carry Wayne State's shared values. Set them in the environment, or let the private Playbook package supply them when the environment is empty, and a fresh app boots against the real services.

Open sesame, minus the incantation. Four settings carry Wayne State's shared values: where the CAS server lives, and who signs the gateway and oauth2 assertions.

| Setting | Config key | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SESAME_CAS_BASE_URL` | `cas.base_url` | The CAS server, an absolute https:// URL. |
| `SESAME_GATEWAY_ISSUER` | `gateway.issuer` | The `iss` claim the gateway assertion must carry. |
| `SESAME_OAUTH2_ISSUER` | `oauth2.issuer` | The `iss` claim the bearer token must carry. |
| `SESAME_OAUTH2_JWKS_URL` | `oauth2.jwks_url` | The URL of the issuer's key set. |

Set them in the environment, as with every other setting. When the environment is empty, the private [waynestate/playbook](https://git.wayne.edu/enterprise-apps/playbook) package supplies the university's values, so a fresh app boots against the real services without a `.env` full of addresses. The environment always wins: a set variable beats the playbook, and an empty one counts as unset.

The playbook is never required. It sits in `suggest`, not `require`, and SESAME runs fine without it, reading these four from the environment alone.

### Get the Playbook[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html#get-the-playbook)

Get it through Composer, fetch the values into a `.env.playbook` file, or clone the repository.

#### Composer[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html#composer)

Add the repository to your `composer.json`:

```json
{
    "repositories": [
        { "type": "vcs", "url": "https://git.wayne.edu/enterprise-apps/playbook.git" }
    ]
}
```

then require it:

```bash
composer require waynestate/playbook
```

Composer keeps the git.wayne.edu credentials it asks for in `auth.json` as an `http-basic` entry, so later installs do not ask again.

#### Fetch the values[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html#fetch-the-values)

**curl (Linux, macOS).**

```bash
curl --fail -H "PRIVATE-TOKEN: $GITLAB_TOKEN" "https://git.wayne.edu/api/v4/projects/enterprise-apps%2Fplaybook/repository/files/playbook.env/raw?ref=main" -o .env.playbook
```

**PowerShell (Windows).**

```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest -Headers @{ 'PRIVATE-TOKEN' = $env:GITLAB_TOKEN } -Uri "https://git.wayne.edu/api/v4/projects/enterprise-apps%2Fplaybook/repository/files/playbook.env/raw?ref=main" -OutFile .env.playbook
```

#### A clone[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html#a-clone)

When the app keeps its private dependencies by hand:

```bash
git clone https://git.wayne.edu/enterprise-apps/playbook.git
```

### Use the values[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/wsu-values.html#use-the-values)

A fetched `.env.playbook` is plain `KEY=value` lines: copy the ones you need into your app's `.env` (or your Citadel environment). SESAME does not read `.env.playbook` itself.

The token is your own: `read_api` for curl, `read_repository` for clone and Composer.

Playbook is private on git.wayne.edu. If you get a 404, ask the Enterprise Applications team for read access.

Raw-PHP apps that build their config by hand can resolve a value the same way the Laravel config does:

```php
use Waynestate\Sesame\Support\Setting;

$baseUrl = Setting::get('SESAME_CAS_BASE_URL'); // env, then playbook, else null
```

- [Which driver for my app?](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html)
- [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html)

[![SESAME's front page: the headline 'The way in. One lock, any key.' and the composer require command beside a pegboard where cas, gateway and SAML keys hang around SESAME's open-door mark, over a green service counter that reads 'Same door for every key.'](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/hero.jpg)](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/index.html)

## SESAME[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#sesame)

![php ^8.3](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/badges/php.svg) ![license MIT](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/badges/license.svg) ![drivers: fake, cas, gateway, oauth2, oidc, saml](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/badges/drivers.svg) [GitHub CI](https://github.com/waynestate/sesame/actions/workflows/ci.yml)

**The way in. One lock, any key.** Single Entry, Sessions App-Managed Everywhere: keys cut while you wait, and no key ever gets to keep the door.

SESAME is Wayne State's protocol-neutral auth library. It returns a verified identity and leaves the session to the app: every driver ends in the same place, the app's `findOrImportUser(Identity)`, and the protocol never holds the session. Switching driver is a config change with no code change. Open sesame.

### Where the code lives[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#where-the-code-lives)

The canonical repository is [enterprise-apps/sesame](https://git.wayne.edu/enterprise-apps/sesame) on git.wayne.edu; issues and merge requests open there, and tags are made there, by the maintainer, with an approver. GitHub ([waynestate/sesame](https://github.com/waynestate/sesame)) is a read-only push mirror; nobody pushes to it, and Packagist reads from it. CI runs on git.wayne.edu.

### Install[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#install)

```
composer require waynestate/sesame
```

### First use[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#first-use)

The quickest way to see it work is the `fake` driver in local development: no server to point at, no registration to make.

```php
<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

require __DIR__.'/vendor/autoload.php';

use Waynestate\Sesame\Config;
use Waynestate\Sesame\DriverFactory;
use Waynestate\Sesame\Identity;
use Waynestate\Sesame\Sesame;
use Waynestate\Sesame\Session\NativeSession;
use Waynestate\Sesame\UserResolver;

session_start();

$config = Config::fromArray([
    'driver' => 'fake',
    'environment' => 'local',
    'fake' => [
        'username' => 'jdoe',
        'attributes' => ['cn' => ['John Doe']],
    ],
]);

$sesame = new Sesame(
    DriverFactory::make($config),
    new class implements UserResolver {
        public function findOrImportUser(Identity $identity): mixed
        {
            return $identity->username;
        }
    },
    new NativeSession(),
    $config,
);

sesame($sesame);

// When the login has not completed, sends the redirect to the identity
// provider and stops the script. When a ticket completes it, sends the
// redirect to the driver's service URL and stops the script, so the ticket
// never stays in the address bar. When the user is already signed in and
// the request has no ticket, returns the user.
$user = sesame_login();
```

Every piece named, and what the app owns and what SESAME does: [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html).

### Pick your path[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/#pick-your-path)

- [Quick start](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html): sign a user in from scratch, one step at a time.
- [Install](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html): what SESAME needs, the composer line, and how to prove it took.
- [Reference](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/drivers.html): the drivers, the configuration, the API, and the proof.

Status: version 0.6.1, MIT license. The changelog's top heading is \[Unreleased\].

Agents: read [llms.txt](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/llms.txt) first; it maps these docs for language models.

---

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html

## Install[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#install)

### Requirements[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#requirements)

- PHP 8.3 or newer (`^8.3`).
- The `simplexml` extension (`ext-simplexml`).
- A PSR-18 HTTP client for the `cas`, `oauth2` and `oidc` drivers (and `saml` with a metadata URL): Guzzle or symfony/http-client. SESAME suggests one, it does not require one.

### Install[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#install-1)

```
composer require waynestate/sesame
```

Note

The `oidc` driver also needs `league/oauth2-client`, which SESAME suggests but does not require: `composer require league/oauth2-client`. Without it, building the driver fails with: `The oidc driver needs league/oauth2-client. Install it with: composer require league/oauth2-client`.

Note

The `saml` driver (opt-in) needs `onelogin/php-saml` 4.3.2 or later, which SESAME suggests but does not require: `composer require onelogin/php-saml`. Older releases are refused, by `composer.json` and when the driver is built.

### Verify[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#verify)

The quickest proof that SESAME is active is a sign-in. In local development, configure the `fake` driver (the [Quick start](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html) walks through it), then call:

```php
$user = sesame_login();
```

Expected: when the login has not completed, SESAME sends the redirect to the identity provider and stops the script; when the user is already signed in and the request has no ticket, it returns the user. With the `fake` driver that is the user your resolver made from the configured username, `jdoe` in the Quick start.

### Next steps[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/install.html#next-steps)

- [Quick start](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html): a first sign-in, one step at a time.
- [Which driver for my app?](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/which-driver.html): pick the key for your door.
- [Raw PHP](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/raw-php.html) and [Laravel](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html): the two ways to wire it in.

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/oidc-library-choice.html

## The oidc driver's library choice[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/oidc-library-choice.html#the-oidc-driver-s-library-choice)

Open sesame needs the right words, and we would rather borrow a maintained dictionary than write our own. This note records which library the `oidc` driver stands on, what else was weighed, and why. Data checked on 2026-10-29 against Packagist (`repo.packagist.org/p2/<package>.json`) and the Packagist security advisory API.

### What the driver needs[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/oidc-library-choice.html#what-the-driver-needs)

- The authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), `state` and `nonce`.
- Discovery from the issuer's `/.well-known/openid-configuration`, cached.
- ID token validation: RSA signature against the issuer's JWKS with an algorithm allowlist, `iss`, `aud`, `azp`, `exp`, `nbf`, `iat`, `nonce`.
- Client authentication with a client secret (`client_secret_post` or `client_secret_basic`), the secret never logged.
- PSR-7/17/18 friendliness, a light dependency tree, PHP 8.3 to 8.5.

SESAME already ships a JWT verifier for the `oauth2` driver (firebase/php-jwt plus `JwksProvider`: cached key set, one refetch per minute for an unknown `kid`, fail closed). A second JWT stack would mean two verifiers to keep correct.

### The candidates[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/oidc-library-choice.html#the-candidates)

| Package | Latest release | PHP | HTTP | PKCE | ID token validation | Weight | Advisories |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| facile-it/php-openid-client | 1.0.0, 2026-06-12 | ^8.2 | PSR-18/17 via php-http/discovery | Not documented in the README | Yes, through web-token/jwt-library and facile-it/php-jose-verifier | Heavy: web-token/jwt-library, php-jose-verifier (which requires symfony/http-client outright), spomky-labs/aes-key-wrap, pki-framework, brick/math, psr/http-server-middleware | None for the package; web-token/jwt-library had four in June 2026, one an algorithm confusion in `JWSVerifier` (fixed in 4.0.7 / 4.1.7) |
| jumbojett/openid-connect-php | v1.0.2, 2024-09-13 | >=7.0 | ext-curl directly, no PSR-18 | Yes | Its own, through phpseclib | Light | None listed |
| league/oauth2-client | 2.9.1, 2026-09-16 | ^7.1 or >=8.0 \<8.6 | Guzzle (required) | Yes, S256 built in since 2.7 | No: OAuth 2.0 only | Light: Guzzle and guzzlehttp/psr7 | None listed |
| thenetworg/oauth2-azure | v2.2.6, 2026-06-22 | ^7.1 or ^8.0 | Guzzle, through league/oauth2-client | Through league | Yes, Azure-specific, with its own key fetching on firebase/php-jwt | league plus Azure-specific code | None listed |

### The choice: league/oauth2-client, plus SESAME's own ID token validation[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/oidc-library-choice.html#the-choice-league-oauth2-client-plus-sesame-s-own-id-token-validation)

- **league/oauth2-client** does the OAuth 2.0 mechanics: the authorization URL, the PKCE verifier and its S256 challenge, the token request with the client's credentials, and the token response parsing. It is the most used OAuth 2.0 client in PHP, released last month, supports PHP up to 8.5, has no published advisories, and its only weight is Guzzle, which the Laravel adapter already uses.
- **SESAME's firebase/php-jwt and `JwksProvider`** validate the ID token, the same code the `oauth2` driver uses for bearer tokens. The OpenID Connect checks league does not do (discovery, `nonce`, `azp`, `iat`, the algorithm allowlist) are a few dozen lines in `src/Drivers/Oidc/IdTokenValidator.php` and `Discovery.php`, written against OpenID Connect Core 3.1.3.7 and Discovery 4.3.

Why not the others:

- **facile-it/php-openid-client** is the most complete OIDC client, but it brings a second JOSE stack (web-token) beside the one SESAME already trusts, that stack had an algorithm confusion advisory this year, and its verifier requires symfony/http-client even when the app uses another PSR-18 client. It is the strongest alternative if SESAME ever needs `private_key_jwt`, encrypted ID tokens or a full relying-party feature set.
- **jumbojett/openid-connect-php** talks to curl directly (no PSR-18, so the tests cannot swap the transport), allows PHP 7.0, and has not had a release since September 2024.
- **thenetworg/oauth2-azure** ties the driver to Azure-specific code and fetches its own keys, duplicating `JwksProvider`. SESAME's driver works with any OpenID provider; Entra is configuration.

### How the dependency is kept optional[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/oidc-library-choice.html#how-the-dependency-is-kept-optional)

league/oauth2-client is in `suggest` and `require-dev`, not `require`, the same way SESAME treats a PSR-18 client. Only the `oidc` driver needs it. When it is missing, building the driver fails with:

```
The oidc driver needs league/oauth2-client. Install it with: composer require league/oauth2-client
```

### Two small layers on top of league[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/oidc-library-choice.html#two-small-layers-on-top-of-league)

- `LeagueProvider` drops league's default `approval_prompt=auto`, a pre-standard parameter OpenID Connect does not define, so the authorization request carries only what the driver chose.
- `BasicAuthOptionProvider` form-encodes the client id and secret before base64 for `client_secret_basic`, as RFC 6749 section 2.3.1 requires; league's own basic provider skips that step.

league's token request goes through Guzzle. When the app's PSR-18 client is Guzzle (the Laravel adapter's default), the driver uses it for the token request too; otherwise it builds a Guzzle client that does not follow redirects and times out after ten seconds.

---

Source: https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html

## API[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#api)

The public surface of waynestate/sesame, named exactly as it is in the code under `src/`: the facade, the factory, the value objects, the ports an app implements, and the global functions the raw-PHP path calls. The incantation is a constructor.

### Classes[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#classes)

Unless noted, everything below is in the `Waynestate\Sesame` namespace.

#### Config[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#config)

The library's config, read from a plain array. `final readonly class Config`.

```php
public static function fromArray(#[\SensitiveParameter] array $config): self
```

Every constructor parameter is a public readonly property, in this order: `driver`, `environment`, `fakeUsername`, `fakeAttributes`, `casBaseUrl`, `casServiceUrl`, `casProtocol`, `casRenew`, `casAssumeMfa`, `sessionIdleMinutes`, `sessionAbsoluteMinutes`, `gatewayHeader`, `gatewayAlgorithm`, `gatewayPublicKey`, `gatewayIssuer`, `gatewayAudience`, `gatewayLeewaySeconds`, `gatewayTrustedProxies`, `gatewayMaxLifetimeSeconds`, `gatewayAllowWithoutReplayGuard`, `oauth2Issuer`, `oauth2JwksUrl`, `oauth2Audience`, `oauth2LeewaySeconds`, `oauth2RequiredScopes`, `oauth2RequiredRoles`, `oauth2IdentityClaim`, `oauth2JwksCacheTtlSeconds`, `oauth2RequireAtJwt`, `oidc` (an `?OidcOptions`), `gatewayPublicKeys`, `gatewayJwksFile` and `saml` (a `?SamlOptions`). Keys, defaults and bounds: see [Configuration](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/configuration.html).

#### DriverFactory[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#driverfactory)

Build a driver from config. `final class DriverFactory`.

```php
public static function make(
    Config $config,
    ?ClientInterface $http = null,
    ?RequestFactoryInterface $requests = null,
    ?ClockInterface $clock = null,
    ?ReplayGuard $replayGuard = null,
    ?CacheInterface $jwksCache = null,
    ?SessionPort $session = null,
): Driver
```

What each argument is for:

- `$http` (PSR-18) and `$requests` (PSR-17): the cas driver talks to a CAS server over HTTP, and the factory cannot build an HTTP client itself, so the app passes both.
- `$clock` (PSR-20): optional, for the cas, gateway and oauth2 drivers' sign-in time; without one they use the system clock.
- `$replayGuard`: the gateway driver needs one (for example a `Psr16ReplayGuard` over a PSR-16 cache), so a captured assertion cannot be replayed. Without one, the gateway driver refuses to start, unless the config says `gateway.allow_without_replay_guard` (local development only).
- `$jwksCache` (PSR-16): the oauth2 driver keeps the fetched key set in it; without one, the oauth2 driver refuses to start. The oidc driver uses it too when passed (discovery document and key set), otherwise it keeps both in process memory.
- `$session`: the oidc driver signs the user in through the browser, so it keeps its state, nonce and PKCE verifier in the app's session. The saml driver keeps its AuthnRequest ID there, and needs `$jwksCache` too: it parks the IdP's posted response in it until the browser comes back with its session cookie.

A missing dependency is an `InvalidConfig` error that names what to pass, and an unknown `driver` value is one too. The oidc driver also needs league/oauth2-client, and the saml driver onelogin/php-saml (4.3.2 or later), which SESAME suggests but does not require. The driver classes themselves live in `Waynestate\Sesame\Drivers`; see [Drivers](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/drivers.html).

#### Sesame[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#sesame)

The facade an app talks to. `final class Sesame`. It holds a driver (or a factory for one, built on first use, so checking a session never pays for the driver's construction), the app's user resolver, the app's session and the config, and it runs the one rule the code holds: every driver ends in `findOrImportUser(Identity)`, and the app owns the session. Time is read through a PSR-20 clock, so the session timeouts are testable.

```php
public function __construct(
    Driver|Closure $driver,
    private readonly UserResolver $resolver,
    private readonly SessionPort $session,
    private readonly Config $config,
    ?ClockInterface $clock = null,
    private readonly ?LoggerInterface $logger = null,
)
```

```php
public function login(ServerRequestInterface $request): mixed
public function returnTo(): ?string
public function serviceUrl(): ?string
public function user(): mixed
public function requireMfa(int $maxAgeSeconds = 28800): MfaResult
public function hasAuthContext(string $id): bool
public function logout(string $returnTo): ?string
public function signOutLocal(): void
public const LOGOUT_TOKEN_FIELD = 'sesame_logout_token'
public const LOGOUT_TOKEN_KEY = 'sesame.logout_token'
public function logoutToken(): string
public function isLogoutToken(#[\SensitiveParameter] mixed $token): bool
public function safeReturnTo(string $returnTo): string
```

- `login()`: returns the `Redirect` unchanged when the user must go to the identity provider. Otherwise it resolves the user: when the resolver returns a user it regenerates the session ID before it stores anything, and returns the user. What it stores is the user, a trimmed identity (username, driver, time, the MFA facts and the authentication contexts, but not the raw IdP attributes, so the session stays small and plain), and the timestamps that start the session's clocks. When the resolver returns null the app has refused the identity: the session is left untouched, nothing is stored, and null is returned, so a refused identity never ends up signed in. An `AuthenticationFailed` from the driver is rethrown unchanged.
- `returnTo()`: where to send the user after the sign-in that just completed, or null when the driver remembers none. Only drivers that implement `RemembersReturnTo` (the oidc and saml drivers) answer, and the value has already passed the `ReturnTo` rule.
- `serviceUrl()`: the driver's configured service URL, or null when the driver has none.
- `user()`: the app's user for the current session, or null when there is none. The session is checked against the timeouts before it is trusted, and a stale session is signed out on the spot, so a stale session can never pass one check and fail another. When the resolver implements `RefreshesUser`, the stored user is looked up again before the answer, and a null result signs the session out, so a deleted account stops reading as signed in from the next request on.
- `requireMfa()`: decides whether the signed-in user's MFA is still good. The session is checked first, through `user()`, so a stale session is signed out before the MFA question is even asked; with no user, or no identity to read, the answer is `NO_AUTH_TIME`: the check fails closed.
- `hasAuthContext()`: decides whether the signed-in identity has the given authentication context, with the same shape and the same fails-closed answer (`false`).
- `logout()`: logs the user out of the app, then points at the identity provider. The app session is invalidated before the provider's URL is built, so a failed redirect can never leave a live session behind; the pointer goes out even when the session holds no user of its own, because the single sign-on session at the provider may still be alive there. Returns the provider's logout URL, or null when the driver has none.
- `signOutLocal()`: clears SESAME's session keys and invalidates the session, without pointing at the identity provider. The guard's logout uses it: the provider's single sign-on session is left alone.
- `logoutToken()`: the logout CSRF token for this session, made on first use (64 hex characters). The raw-PHP logout (`sesame_logout()`) only runs for a POST that carries this token, so another site cannot sign the user out with a link or a hidden form. Laravel apps use Laravel's own CSRF token instead (the logout route is in the web middleware group).
- `isLogoutToken()`: whether the given token is this session's logout CSRF token. A session that never made one accepts nothing.
- `safeReturnTo()`: the safe URL to send the user to after logout. The return-to must be an absolute https URL on the service URL's scheme, host and port; anything else sends the user to the service URL instead, so a logout can never be turned into an open redirect.
- `LOGOUT_TOKEN_FIELD`: the form field the raw-PHP logout reads its CSRF token from. `LOGOUT_TOKEN_KEY`: the session key that holds the logout CSRF token.

When a logger is set, sign-in and sign-out events are logged through it: a broken logger never changes what the facade returns or throws, and no ticket, session ID, token, assertion, cookie or header ever reaches the log.

#### Identity[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#identity)

The verified identity a driver hands to the resolver. `final readonly class Identity`; the constructor refuses an empty username with `InvalidArgumentException`.

```php
public function __construct(
    public string $username,
    public array $attributes,
    public string $driver,
    public DateTimeImmutable $authenticatedAt,
    public ?DateTimeImmutable $authTime = null,
    public array $amr = [],
    private array $authContexts = [],
)
```

- `attribute(string $name): ?string`: the first value of one attribute, or null when the attribute is absent.
- `isFromNewLogin(): ?bool`: read from the CAS `isFromNewLogin` attribute: true for the string "true" (any case), false for "false", and null when the attribute is absent or carries any other value. Drivers that do not release the attribute answer null; the identity never invents one.
- `usedLongTermToken(): ?bool`: the same shape, read from the CAS `longTermAuthenticationRequestTokenUsed` attribute.
- `authContexts(): array`: the authentication contexts verified for this sign-in, in the order the driver reported them. Empty when no step-up was required.
- `hasAuthContext(string $id): bool`: whether this sign-in verified the given authentication context: a membership test on the list, never an equality on the whole list.

#### LoginStep, Authenticated, Redirect[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#loginstep-authenticated-redirect)

A login ends in one of two shapes, both `final` and both extending the `abstract class LoginStep`, which is empty on purpose:

```php
final class Authenticated extends LoginStep
{
    public function __construct(
        public readonly Identity $identity,
    ) {}
}

final class Redirect extends LoginStep
{
    public function __construct(
        public readonly string $url,
    ) {}
}
```

`Authenticated`: the identity is verified; this is who the user is. `Redirect`: send the user to this URL to continue the login.

#### Driver[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#driver)

One way to verify an identity. A driver knows one protocol and nothing about the app: it turns a request into a `LoginStep`, and the core does the rest. Switching driver is a config change with no code change.

```php
interface Driver
{
    public function name(): string;
    public function login(ServerRequestInterface $request): LoginStep;
    public function logoutUrl(string $returnTo): ?string;
    public function serviceUrl(): ?string;
}
```

`logoutUrl()` is the identity provider's logout URL, or null when the driver has none; `serviceUrl()` is the configured service URL, or null, and it is the host a logout return-to must stay on.

#### UserResolver, RefreshesUser, RemembersReturnTo[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#userresolver-refreshesuser-remembersreturnto)

The port the app implements, and the optional extras a resolver or driver can use:

```php
interface UserResolver
{
    public function findOrImportUser(Identity $identity): mixed;
}

interface RefreshesUser
{
    public function refreshUser(mixed $user): mixed;
}

interface RemembersReturnTo
{
    public function returnTo(): ?string;
}
```

`UserResolver` is the one place every driver ends: turn a verified identity into the app's user, or return null to refuse it. `RefreshesUser` lets the app look the stored user up again on every `user()` call. `RemembersReturnTo` lets a driver remember where to send the user after the sign-in that just completed.

#### Session[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#session)

The app's session, seen through a port:

```php
interface SessionPort
{
    public function regenerate(): void;
    public function get(string $key): mixed;
    public function put(string $key, mixed $value): void;
    public function forget(string $key): void;
    public function invalidate(): void;
}
```

`Waynestate\Sesame\Session\NativeSession` is the port over the native PHP session. It never starts a session and never sets cookie flags: starting the session is the app's job (`session_start()`), and hardening the session cookie is HELMET's job. It reads and writes `$_SESSION` on a session that is already active, and throws `LogicException` when it is not. `invalidate()` is the one operation that ends the session: it clears the data, expires the cookie on the client, and retires the session, so a stolen ID is dead after logout.

#### MFA[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#mfa)

The one rule that decides whether an identity's MFA is still good. `final class Mfa`:

```php
public const MFA_METHODS = ['mfa', 'otp', 'hwk', 'swk', 'fido', 'sms', 'pop'];
public const FUTURE_SKEW_SECONDS = 60;
public static function satisfied(Identity $identity, int $maxAgeSeconds, DateTimeImmutable $now): MfaResult
```

An identity satisfies MFA only when the identity provider reported a sign-in time (`auth_time`), that time is recent enough, and the sign-in used an MFA method (`amr`). Anything the provider did not report is treated as missing, so the check fails closed: a driver that carries no MFA facts is always denied. The checks run in a fixed order, so the reason is stable:

1. no `auth_time`: `NO_AUTH_TIME`
2. `auth_time` more than 60 seconds in the future: `FUTURE_AUTH_TIME`
3. `auth_time` older than `$maxAgeSeconds`: `TOO_OLD`
4. no MFA method in `amr`: `NO_MFA_METHOD`
5. otherwise: `SATISFIED`

A sign-in exactly `$maxAgeSeconds` old is still satisfied.

`final readonly class MfaResult` carries the answer:

```php
public const SATISFIED = 'SATISFIED';
public const NO_AUTH_TIME = 'NO_AUTH_TIME';
public const NO_MFA_METHOD = 'NO_MFA_METHOD';
public const TOO_OLD = 'TOO_OLD';
public const FUTURE_AUTH_TIME = 'FUTURE_AUTH_TIME';
public function __construct(
    public bool $satisfied,
    public string $reason,
)
public function message(): string
```

`message()` is the human form of the result, for a message or a log line.

#### ReturnTo[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#returnto)

The one rule for a return-to URL (after login or logout). `final class ReturnTo`:

```php
public static function safe(string $returnTo, ?string $serviceUrl): string
```

A return-to must be an absolute URL on the same origin as the service URL: the same scheme, the same host and the same effective port (443 for https, 80 for http, when none is written), with no user name or password in it. The scheme must be https; plain http is allowed only for a localhost or 127.0.0.1 service URL, for local development. Anything else sends the user to the service URL instead, so a login or logout can never be turned into an open redirect, not even to another port on the same host. When the driver has no service URL there is nothing to check against, so the return-to is used as-is.

#### OidcOptions[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#oidcoptions)

`Waynestate\Sesame\Drivers\Oidc\OidcOptions`: the `oidc` config block, validated. `final readonly class OidcOptions`.

```php
public const ALLOWED_ALGORITHMS = ['RS256', 'RS384', 'RS512'];
public const CLIENT_AUTH_METHODS = ['client_secret_post', 'client_secret_basic'];
public const MAX_CACHE_TTL_SECONDS = 3600;
public static function fromArray(#[\SensitiveParameter] array $oidc): self
public function clientSecret(): string
```

The keys, their environment variables and their defaults are in the oidc table on the [Configuration page](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/configuration.html).

#### SamlOptions and SamlDriver[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#samloptions-and-samldriver)

`Waynestate\Sesame\Drivers\Saml\SamlOptions`: the `saml` config block, validated at boot (certificates, the key and a metadata file are read from their paths then). `final readonly class SamlOptions`.

```php
public const DEFAULT_ATTRIBUTES = [/* accessid, email, name, affiliations, eppn */];
public const DEFAULT_MFA_CONTEXTS = ['https://refeds.org/profile/mfa'];
public static function fromArray(#[\SensitiveParameter] array $saml): self
public function spKey(): ?string
```

`Waynestate\Sesame\Drivers\SamlDriver` implements `Driver` and `RemembersReturnTo`, and adds the two endpoints the other drivers do not have:

```php
public const LIBRARY_FLOOR = '4.3.2';
public const XMLSECLIBS_FLOOR = '3.1.5';
public const HANDLE_PARAM = 'saml_handle';
public function receive(ServerRequestInterface $request): Redirect // the ACS; send as 303
public function metadata(): string                                  // the SP metadata XML
public function acsUrl(): string
public static function assertLibraryInstalled(string $class = self::LIBRARY_CLASS): void
```

The keys are in [the saml driver guide](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/driver-saml.html#config-keys).

#### Setting[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#setting)

`Waynestate\Sesame\Support\Setting`: the one lookup for the library's shared settings. The real environment wins (getenv, then $\_ENV, then $\_SERVER); when it has nothing, the private waynestate/playbook package supplies Wayne State's shared values when it is installed. An empty value counts as missing, so a blank variable never shadows the playbook.

```php
public const ENVIRONMENT_ONLY = ['SESAME_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET'];
public static function get(string $key): ?string
public static function env(string $key): ?string
```

`get()` answers from the environment, then the playbook, else null. `env()` answers from the environment only, and the playbook is never consulted. A key in `ENVIRONMENT_ONLY` never falls back to the playbook, so a shared package can never supply an app's secret.

### Functions[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#functions)

Plain functions in the global namespace behind a `sesame_` prefix, the same shape as WayneUI's standalone path, because that is what a framework-free application can consume. Each one is guarded with `function_exists`, so two copies of this file can never collide. The app owns the session: start it with `session_start()` before calling anything here, and let HELMET set the cookie flags.

```php
function sesame(?Sesame $instance = null): Sesame
function sesame_request(): ServerRequestInterface
function sesame_login(): mixed
function sesame_user(): mixed
function sesame_require_mfa(int $maxAgeSeconds = 28800): mixed
function sesame_require_context(string $id): mixed
function sesame_logout_token(): string
function sesame_logout(string $returnTo): void
function sesame_saml_acs(SamlDriver $driver): never
function sesame_saml_metadata(SamlDriver $driver): never
```

- `sesame()`: hold the one `Sesame` instance for this process. Set it once at boot, read it after: `sesame($sesame);` then `sesame();`. Reading it with none set throws `LogicException`.
- `sesame_request()`: build the PSR-7 request for the current request from the globals. The PSR-17 factories come from nyholm/psr7, which the library already requires, so the raw-PHP path needs nothing but the autoloader.
- `sesame_login()`: run a login against the current request. When the driver answers with a `Redirect`, sends the 302 and stops the script, so no protected code runs after the redirect. A request that already has a user and no ticket returns that user without calling the driver, so a page that calls it on every request cannot bounce the signed-in user back to the identity provider in a loop. When a ticket completes the login, the user is sent to the driver's service URL (or the checked return-to the oidc sign-in began with) and the script stops, so the ticket never stays in the address bar. When the resolver refuses the identity, null is returned and no redirect is sent: the ticket is single-use, so leaving it in that one refused URL is harmless. The oidc driver's callback (a request with `state` and a `code` or an `error`) and the saml driver's return from the ACS (a request with `saml_handle`) count as a ticket here, and a request with `step_up=1` always goes to the driver too, so a signed-in user can be asked for a fresh sign-in.
- `sesame_user()`: the app's user for the current session, or null when there is none.
- `sesame_require_mfa()`: require that the signed-in user's MFA is still good. When it is satisfied, the app's user is returned, so a protected page can read the user and the MFA proof in one call; when it is not, `MfaNotSatisfied` is thrown, carrying the result with the stable reason and the human message.
- `sesame_require_context()`: require that the signed-in identity has the given authentication context. When it does, the app's user is returned; when it does not, `AuthContextNotSatisfied` is thrown, carrying the context id.
- `sesame_logout_token()`: the logout CSRF token for this session, for the logout form. The token is hex, so it needs no escaping in HTML:

```php
<form method="post" action="/logout.php">
  <input type="hidden" name="sesame_logout_token" value="<?= sesame_logout_token() ?>">
  <button>Sign out</button>
</form>
```

- `sesame_logout()`: log the user out, then send them on. Invalidates the app session, redirects to the identity provider's logout URL when the driver has one, otherwise to the safe return-to, and stops the script, so no protected code runs after the redirect. CSRF guard: the logout runs only for a POST whose body carries the session's token in the `sesame_logout_token` field. A GET answers 405 with `Allow: POST`, and a POST without the right token answers 403; both leave the session alone and stop the script, so another site cannot sign the user out with an image, a link or a forged form. The response carries `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Clear-Site-Data: "cache", "storage"`; `cookies` is deliberately left out, so the user is not signed out of every other app on the host.
- `sesame_saml_acs()`: the saml driver's ACS page. Parks the IdP's POST and answers 303 to the login URL, or a plain 400 for a POST it cannot use, then stops the script. Call it on a page that does NOT call `session_start()`: the IdP's cross-site POST carries no `SameSite=Lax` session cookie, and a session started there would replace the user's real one.
- `sesame_saml_metadata()`: sends the SP metadata as `application/samlmetadata+xml` and stops the script. It needs no session.

### Exceptions[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#exceptions)

The exceptions an app meets, in `Waynestate\Sesame\Exception`:

- `AuthenticationFailed`: a driver could not verify the identity. The message can carry the ticket or other provider details, so it is never logged and should not be shown: log it for operators and show the user one generic line.
- `MfaNotSatisfied`: the MFA check is not satisfied; carries the `MfaResult` with the stable reason and the human message.
- `AuthContextNotSatisfied`: the identity lacks the authentication context; carries the context id.
- `InvalidConfig`: a config error at boot: a missing or invalid key from `Config::fromArray()`, or a driver missing the dependency `DriverFactory::make()` needs.
- `FakeDriverInProduction`: the `fake` driver refuses to boot in production.

### Where the rest lives[#](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/api.html#where-the-rest-lives)

- The driver implementations: `Waynestate\Sesame\Drivers` (`CasDriver`, `FakeDriver`, `GatewayDriver`, `OAuth2Driver`, `OidcDriver`, `SamlDriver`, `ReplayGuard`, `Psr16ReplayGuard`), documented on the [Drivers](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/drivers.html) page.
- The Laravel adapter: `Waynestate\Sesame\Laravel` (`SesameServiceProvider`, `SesameGuard`, `Authenticate`, `RequireMfa`, `RequireAuthContext`, `LaravelSession`, `LaravelPsr16Cache`), documented in the [Laravel guide](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/laravel.html).
- The wayne-cas compatibility layer: `Waynestate\Sesame\WayneCas`, documented in [Moving from wayne-cas](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/moving-from-wayne-cas.html).
- The Wayne Auth bridge: `Waynestate\Sesame\WayneAuth\WayneAuth` (deprecated on arrival), documented in [Moving off Wayne Auth](https://sesame.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/moving-off-wayne-auth.html).
